pre_change_state.caveat_quote: The database seems to under-represent recent work: I found almost no field studies of Pepper, and nothing on ElliQ.

claims.text: | Moyle et al. 2017 cluster-RCT [W2778691880] | Long-term care. PARO compared with a plush toy and usual care. | This record is a qualitative reflection on five participants, not the main outcomes. It reports large individual variation in response and ethical questions about giving PARO and taking it away. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract: qualitative reflection on five participants, variation in response, ethics of giving/retrieving PARO; trial compared PARO, plush toy, usual care in long-term care.

claims.text: | Jøranson et al. 2020 [W3088196398] | Cluster RCT, 60 residents with dementia, 10 Norwegian nursing homes. PARO group activity twice a week for 12 weeks. | Actigraphy-measured sleep improved in the PARO group: higher sleep efficiency and total sleep time, fewer night awakenings. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Matches abstract: cluster RCT, 60 participants, 10 NHs, twice weekly 12 weeks, improved sleep efficiency, total sleep time, fewer awakenings.

claims.text: **Narrative findings.** The narrative synthesis suggested improvements in engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and reductions in loneliness and medication use [W2808281222].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract states narrative review indicated improved engagement, interaction, stress indicators, reduced loneliness and medication use.

claims.text: **PARO versus a stuffed animal in occupational therapy** [W4407738599].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: The paper compares PARO with a stuffed animal in occupational therapy.

claims.text: **Consistent results.** Engagement, positive affect and social interaction (including with staff) recur across designs [W2732925385, W1505024467, W2894885829, W2040979576].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Each of the four studies reports engagement/affect/social interaction findings, including communication with staff (Liang).

claims.text: | Wada & Shibata 2007 [W2043711811]; one-year follow-up [W2148142846] | Seal robots in a Japanese care house and a health service facility for the aged. | More social interaction and improved urinary stress-hormone reactions. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Wada 2007 shows increased social interaction and improved urinary stress reactions; the 2006 study is a one-year follow-up at a health service facility; Japanese setting is plausible but 'Japanese' is not stated, though minor.

claims.text: **Pepper.** The only Pepper-related hit is a protocol comparing a humanoid robot with tablet training for people with dementia at home [W2975531399].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Protocol compares humanoid Pepper with tablet training for people with dementia at home.

claims.text: | Jøranson 2020 [W3088196398]; thesis [W3102212853] | Cluster RCT. 60 residents, 10 Norwegian nursing-home special care units. PARO group sessions twice a week for 12 weeks. | Actigraphy showed better sleep: higher sleep efficiency and total sleep time, and fewer awakenings. The thesis also covers agitation, depression, psychotropic drugs and quality of life, but the abstract I retrieved doesn't give those results. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Sleep results match W3088196398, and the thesis abstract lists agitation, depression, drugs and QoL as investigated without results.

claims.text: **Jibo-style robot in assisted living (lead).** An assisted-living study aimed at community-level connection between residents [W2943699887].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: The record never mentions Jibo; it only describes a social robot in assisted-living community engagement.

claims.text: Attachment did not explain the loneliness reduction [W2132164645].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract says attachment was not the mechanism for decreased loneliness.

claims.text: | [W3015603533] Taiwan PARO study | Participants were older adults with depression. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Participants were twenty older adults with depression in Taiwan, using Paro.

claims.text: | [W2159536297] AIBO "early dementia" | Participants had MMSE above 23, so mild deficits at most. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Participants had MMSE>23, mild deficits.

claims.text: **Robotic cat versus plush cat, special care unit** [W2074069593].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Pilot compared robotic cat and plush cat in a special care unit.

claims.text: Data reliability was 99.6% and usability averaged 80.1/100 [W2946005838].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract gives 99.6% reliability and usability 80.1.

claims.text: **Risk of bias.** Risk of bias was high, particularly for allocation concealment and blinding [W2808281222].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract: risk of bias relatively high in allocation concealment and blinding.

claims.text: | [W2717439789] Companion robot in homes | Eight self-supporting seniors living alone. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Eight senior volunteers living alone and self-supporting in home field test.

claims.text: **Chat robot in COVID-era care.** A "Sunshine" chat robot pilot for older adults with cognitive impairment [W3041860695].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Title and abstract refer to Sunshine chat robot pilot for older adults with cognitive impairment during COVID-19.

claims.text: This is a conference abstract and a lead [W2982896790, W2899915867].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Records are Innovation in Aging abstracts; 'conference abstract' status isn't stated, and the 'lead' characterization is not a paper claim.

claims.text: | Liang et al. 2017 [W2732925385] | Pilot block RCT, 30 dyads, 2 dementia day centres in Auckland plus participants' homes, 12 weeks. | Better facial affect and more communication with staff at the day centres. Participants with less cognitive impairment responded better. No significant differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: All details match the Liang abstract.

claims.text: **PARO, NAO and a real dog, Spain** [W1807810766].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Study applied NAO, PARO and a dog; Spain is plausible from authors but not stated; core matches.

claims.text: | Valentí Soler et al. 2015 [W1807810766] | Quasi-experimental, about 100 nursing-home patients per phase plus day-care patients. 3 months. PARO, NAO and a real dog compared with control. | Apathy improved in the robot groups. Quality-of-life (QUALID) scores rose with PARO. The NAO group declined on one cognition measure (MMSE). Day-care results were mixed. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Apathy improved, QUALID rose in PARO, NAO MMSE decline, mixed day care; ~100 per phase.

claims.text: **PARO in a nursing-home public area, 3 months** [W2039822570].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Three-month field study with PARO in nursing home public area.

claims.text: | [W2294211165] Dog, PARO and toy cat visits | Mixed nursing-home residents, with dementia diagnoses recorded but not required. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dog, PARO, toy cat visits to nursing-home residents; dementia diagnoses were collected.

claims.text: **Exercise coach.** Fasola & Matarić's robot coach (two user studies with older adults) showed a strong preference for a relational over a non-relational coach, with high usability ratings [W2065178260].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract reports strong preference for relational coach and high ratings.

claims.text: | [W2112421347] Brian 2.1 at mealtimes | Eight residents aged 82–93, with no cognitive status given. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Eight individuals aged 82-93; cognitive status not given.

claims.text: | [W1945345301] Broadbent multi-robot trial | General aged-care residents and staff. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Aged care facility residents and staff in nonrandomised trial with multiple robots.

claims.text: [W2003566851] Memory game case study in long-term care.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Memory game case study with Brian 2.1 at long-term care facility.

claims.text: **Targeted outcomes.** The newer, more specific RCTs report effects on sleep [W3088196398] and on pain and PRN medication use [W3097289914].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Sleep effects in W3088196398 and pain/PRN medication effects in W3097289914.

claims.text: Broadbent's multi-robot trial in a general aged-care facility [W1945345301].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Broadbent trial in aged care facility with multiple robots.

claims.text: **Weak or null results.** Broad dementia-symptom, caregiver-burden and physiological measures often showed no difference [W2732925385, W2955051104, W2995685337].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: All three report no significant differences or limited effects on dementia symptoms, caregiver well-being, or physiological measures.

claims.text: **Joy for All robot animals, 6-month diary study** [W3015009700].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Six-month diary study with Joy for All robot animals.

claims.text: Its sibling, the observational PARO study [W2039822570], is in the dementia map as a borderline inclusion.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Refers to the observational PARO study, which exists; 'dementia map' is process commentary.

claims.text: A related review is the telepresence-for-dementia integrative review [W2751864896].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: W2751864896 is an integrative review of telepresence robots for dementia.

claims.text: **Matilda and similar baby-face robots in Australian residential care** [W2564685734, W2317990020].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Both studies concern Matilda and Sophie/Jack baby-face robots in Australian residential care.

claims.text: | [W2898061611] Japanese quasi-experimental study (ICF framework) | 67 nursing-home residents aged 65+ with three robot types. Dementia isn't mentioned. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: 67 residents aged 65+, three robot types, ICF; dementia not mentioned.

claims.text: **Implementation.** Staff time, reliability, infection control and individual variation recur as practical issues [W2915888239, W3081435517, W2778691880].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Zora paper reports start-up time and software failure barriers, microbial paper infection control, Moyle individual variation.

claims.text: [W2789445850] Scoping review of socially assistive robots in elderly care.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: W2789445850 is a scoping review of SAR in elderly care.

claims.text: | Moyle cluster-RCT [W2778691880] | PARO compared with a plush toy and usual care in long-term care. | The record I could retrieve is a qualitative reflection on five participants, not the main outcomes. It reports large variation in response, including different responses from the same person over time, and ethical issues around giving and withdrawing PARO. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Matches the qualitative reflection: variation, same individual different responses, ethics of giving and retrieving.

claims.text: See also AIBO versus animal-assisted therapy in dementia [W1972564462] and an earlier robocat inquiry [W2074069593].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: W1972564462 is not among the records, so the AIBO vs AAT claim cannot be verified; the robocat inquiry part is fine.

claims.text: | [W2915888239] Zora in Dutch nursing homes | The abstract doesn't specify client groups. |
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Zora abstract does not specify client groups beyond residential care.

observations.caveat_quote: I could not retrieve the main outcome paper of the Moyle cluster-RCT, which is the largest PARO trial against a plush-toy control. Search for it directly.
